series.note: Rescued includes 252 foreign nationals and 3,344 lifted by helicopter.

NDRRMA SitRep #01, 09:00 NPT. Bodies recovered from eight districts along the Bhote Koshi-Trishuli basin. Missing reported across 62 districts nationally. Rescued includes 253 foreign nationals and 3,702 lifted by helicopter. Injured is 279 treated across 16 facilities. OCHA Flash Update #5 and press reporting gave 1,003 dead for the same morning; the two are not reconciled.
Missing stated as approximately 5,000, including about 600 foreign nationals from 35 countries. Rescued includes 300+ foreign nationals.

MoFA daily update, 14:00 NPT. Missing approximately 5,300 including about 600 foreign nationals from 35 countries; rescued includes 300+ foreign nationals. Confirms two Nepali tunnel survivors from Upper Trishuli 3A (4 Sep) and one Chinese national from Upper Trishuli 1 (5 Sep); SAR teams from India, China, South Korea, UAE, Malaysia and Australia active in tunnel rescue.
As of 18:00. No injured or rescued figure restated in this update.

NDRRMA spokesperson Shanti Mahat, 14:52 NPT, via Khabarhub. Missing decreased from the 8 Sep figure, consistent with reclassification from missing to recovered rather than a data error. 102 bodies identified and returned to families; 3,628 people in holding centres across Nuwakot, Dhading, Rasuwa and Kathmandu; 7,151 people received medical treatment, a broader/cumulative figure not the same category as the 279 injured figure from 1 Sep.

china.detail: Gyirong (Kyirong) county, Tibet Autonomous Region. Missing includes about 261 foreign nationals. Xinhua reported 31 dead and 531 missing as of 4 September.
china.note: Tracked entirely separately from Nepal's national count. No NDRRMA or MoFA figure includes these people.

alternates.label: Nepal Tourism Board
alternates.detail: 644 travellers unaccounted for in total: 517 foreign nationals and 127 Nepalis.

foreign_nationals.note: Three official counts taken on different dates by different agencies; they do not agree. India is the largest single nationality reported, revised upward from 178 to 288 across updates.

notes: The headline figure is bodies recovered, not identified deaths. Only about 4% of the roughly 900 bodies found by 1 September had been formally identified; forensic teams from India, China, Japan, Singapore and South Korea were still working as of 7 September.
Missing is a separate category and is not presumed dead. NDRRMA's own language treats these people as unlocated, and the count is not additive with bodies recovered without that caveat.

District counts reflect where a body was found, not where the person lived or died. Bodies travelled up to 240 km downstream, which is why Chitwan (363) and the two Nawalparasi districts (445 combined) show higher recovered-body counts than the upstream epicentre districts of Rasuwa and Nuwakot.
The often-quoted ~900 figure is the 31 August snapshot, not a competing method. It is the same count at an earlier date.
No consolidated official injured count was published after 31 August 2026, and no national displaced-household total was found on any primary government page.

NDRRMA issued later situation reports, including #7 dated 7 September 19:00 and an update on 8 September, but none of those PDFs could be retrieved. Figures dated after 1 September therefore come from MoFA daily updates and named press reporting rather than an NDRRMA document.
The SitRep #01 missing-persons breakdown by category is published as an infographic that could not be read back reliably, so no category split is shown here.

NDRRMA's 9 September update (14:52 NPT, spokesperson Shanti Mahat, via Khabarhub) broke the missing down by category: 45 Nepali Army personnel, 25 Nepal Police personnel, 12 Armed Police Force personnel, 73 government employees, 26 bank/financial institution employees and about 589 foreign tourists. The same update reported 102 bodies identified and returned to families, and 3,628 people in holding centres across Nuwakot, Dhading, Rasuwa and Kathmandu.

NDRRMA's 9 September figure of 7,151 people who received medical treatment is a broader, likely cumulative count. It is not the same category as the 279 injured figure from 1 September and does not replace it.
IOM appealed on 8 September for USD 20.5 million to assist 43,000 of an estimated 84,000 people affected by the floods, as part of the Government of Nepal-led response.

summary.text: Ready-to-eat food delivered; rice, lentils and solar batteries still required. Named with Aamachhodingmo as one of the two most severely affected local levels: 3,702 households and 14,461 people isolated for up to six days, of them 3,650 children and 1,204 older people. Syafrubesi and Timure health posts and the Timure health desk were fully damaged.

summary.text: Ready-to-eat food delivered; rice, lentils and solar batteries still required. All wards were cut off from the road network and ward 1 was directly flood-hit. Only ward 1 had grid power by 6 September, with four wards still dark.

wards_official.text: All wards cut off from the road network; ward 1 directly flood-affected

summary.text: Minimum food supplies had reached; a shortage of tents was causing shelter difficulties, with rice, lentils and solar batteries still required. The Mailung Community Health Unit was fully damaged, and the Trishuli-Mailung-Syabrubesi road at Khalte in ward 5 was completely and persistently obstructed.
Ready-to-eat food delivered to all locations; rice, lentils and solar batteries still required.

Disinfectant and chemicals were needed to control the odour from dead animals and human remains. Twenty-four bodies were found in a single house at Betrawati in ward 10; between Sole Bazar and Akkare Bazar in ward 7 houses were washed away, two concrete bridges destroyed and more than 200 residents were out of contact. The Bidur water supply project lost 4.5 km of pipeline and three sump wells, affecting about 4,000 households, and a wastewater treatment plant was destroyed.
Four holding centres were open. The Pasang Lhamu road at Simtar in ward 10 was completely obstructed. Site of the Trishuli Galchhi project. No municipality-level casualty figure was published.
No shelter facilities and no relief had reached the municipality. Immediate relief was needed at Belkotgadhi, Mahadevsthan and Ratamate.

Minimum essential supplies available, but road access and electricity were unresolved. The municipality requested 50 to 60 solar units, was procuring its own medical supplies, and asked for the rest by helicopter.
Two bridges on the Tadi Khola were destroyed.

Drinking water needed. The Prithvi Highway is fully blocked at Krishnabhir, where about 70 m of road foundation collapsed into the Trishuli, and again at Parewabhir; the Mugling-Kathmandu section is closed both directions. About half of a 300 m bypass track had opened by early September before new slope cracks were found above the worksite. The Phurke Khola bridge at Malekhu was also washed away.

Three hundred metres of 50 mm pipe was needed to restore drinking water to about 100 households in ward 1. Baireni Hospital was partially damaged. The municipality is also the hub of the reopened right-bank detour to Trishuli Bazar.
Downstream municipality on the Trishuli. No municipality-level figure published; Chitwan's 363 recovered bodies are a district total and reflect where remains were found, not local deaths.
Downstream municipality on the Narayani. No municipality-level figure published.
The Tokha-Chhahare road at Ghattekhola in ward 8 was placed under a 22:00 to 05:00 night restriction.

Used by NEA to reroute power, stepped down to 11 kV for local feeders. Active and carrying emergency restoration load.
Not detailed in the sources checked; damage is implied by the destruction of the Chilime powerhouse but no figure was published.

restoration.note: Nepal Energy Forum gives 83% for the same date; the two are not reconciled.
OnlineKhabar separately reports about 90% for the same date.
About 120 families still without power. The Kathmandu Post described this as nearly all households on 6 September.

restoration.detail: 500 portable 2 kW household solar units and 13 institutional solar systems distributed through the Alternative Energy Promotion Centre; 1,268 vulnerable Rasuwa households flagged for solar.

restoration.note: Ministry of Energy figure, confirming Nepal Energy Forum's earlier 83% reading (vs Kathmandu Post's 78% for 6 September, also in this table).
Ministry of Energy figure. Lower than the 96.7% reported for 6 September; likely a denominator or rounding difference between agencies rather than a real regression — not reconciled.

impact.text: Nepal became a net electricity exporter for the first time in about a decade in the fiscal year ending mid-July 2026, earning Rs 18.75 bn from sales to India and Bangladesh. Officials expect that to reverse in the winter low-flow season and have sought advance import approvals from India effective September 2026.
India agreed to supply advance power to Nepal to cope with the flood, ahead of the normal schedule.

Loss estimates diverge sharply. IPPAN puts hydropower-sector losses at Rs 25-30 bn, roughly a quarter to a third of affected project costs; NEA's preliminary assessment says hundreds of billions of rupees; the Finance Minister attributed Rs 100 bn specifically to hydro infrastructure within a Rs 900 bn economy-wide rebuilding figure.

Missing-worker counts across the energy sector were revised sharply downward as rescue and contact efforts progressed: 933 (NDRRMA), 898 at 11 projects (IPPAN, 29 August), 983 out of contact against 639 officially counted missing, and by 7 September the Nepal Army believed 121 people were still trapped in hydropower tunnels.

road.detail: Betrawati-Rasuwagadhi road (42 km) destroyed at multiple points; no reopening date and authorities advise against travel.
Miteri Friendship Bridge and the border customs post destroyed on 26 August.
16 km section toward the China border damaged; market area flood-hit on 26 August. A 75 m Bailey bridge span is needed here.
Bogatitar-Kalikasthan-Dhunche section reopened to light four-wheel-drive only; the Bidur-Dhunche road was limited to small 4WD vehicles.

displacement_site.detail: Relief supplies staged here; onward delivery to villages is the bottleneck.

road.detail: Passable in daylight only, with a mandatory night closure enforced. (unofficial)
Trishuli-Mailung-Syabrubesi road washed away; helicopter access only for relief.
Roads to Simle and Shanti Bazaar wiped out; no access to shops, hospitals or government offices.

Bailey bridge not yet started as of 8-9 Sep; the Nepal Army bridging team is due to move to Betrawati immediately after finishing Devighat. About 1.5 km of track remains to be opened between Dhunge Bazar and Betrawati before installation can begin.

power.detail: Not reported separately from the Nuwakot district figure.

road.detail: Old and new Trishuli Bazar bridges swept away. A 48 m Bailey bridge is planned but not yet installed.

telecom.detail: Ncell tower still down in the Trishuli/Bidur area.

road.detail: Reachable via the reopened Galchhi detour; the direct Trishuli-Betrawati road is still damaged.

water.detail: Bidur Water Supply Project running on a 100 kVA diesel generator, distributing about 500,000 litres a day. A short-term measure, not a restoration.

road.detail: Nepal Army-built 60 m Acrow bridge over the Tadi river (5.5 m wide, 50-tonne capacity, built in five days by a 55-member Bridging Unit team) opened to pedestrians from 10 Sep; vehicle traffic due to resume from 11 Sep.
Terminus of the Galchhi detour route toward Trishuli Bazar; open as a narrow single-lane track.
Hub of the reopened right-bank detour road, the alternative to the destroyed Trishuli-corridor bridges.
Phurke Khola bridge washed away, with local road damage.

Prithvi Highway fully blocked at Krishnabhir by a 70 m road-foundation collapse into the Trishuli; the Muglin-Kathmandu section is closed both ways. About 50 m of a 300 m bypass track had opened before new slope cracks were found above the worksite.
All wards reported inaccessible by road.

power.detail: Only ward 1 has power; four wards remain dark.

corridor.text: Pasang Lhamu Highway (NH42), Betrawati to Rasuwagadhi: 42 km damaged at multiple points with several concrete bridges washed away, plus a further 16 km from Syabrubesi toward the China border. No confirmed reopening date; authorities advise against travel to Rasuwagadhi, Timure or Kerung until the route is reassessed.

NDRRMA listed ten obstructed road sections on 1 September: the Prithvi Highway completely blocked at Krishnabhir and Parewabhir on the Mugling-Dhading section and blocked again on Mugling-Malekhu; Galchhi-Devighat and Devighat-Dhunge blocked; the Trishuli-Mailung-Syabrubesi road completely and persistently obstructed at Khalte in Uttargaya-5; all main highways in Rasuwa closed until further notice; the Pasang Lhamu road completely obstructed at Simtar in Belkotgadhi-10; night restrictions on the Tokha-Chhahare road at Ghattekhola in Shivapuri-8 and on the B.P. Highway in Kavre; and the Kanti Lokpath blocked by a landslide at Bhattedanda in Lalitpur.

Prithvi Highway is closed both directions at Krishnabhir in Benighat Rorang, Dhading, where about 70 m of road foundation collapsed into the Trishuli. A 300 m bypass track is under construction, roughly half open, but seven cracks up to 15 m long were found in the slope above the worksite. The Prime Minister said the section would reopen within September.

Detour in use: Galchhi to Kalleritar, Koshikhola, Piplatar, Darshantar, Chhatrekhola and Gauribesi along the right bank of the Trishuli. It restores a rough single-lane connection from Dhading and Galchhi to Trishuli Bazar without crossing the destroyed river bridges, but is narrow, slow and hard for two-way traffic.

Bailey bridges planned by the Department of Roads at four locations: Devighat in Bidur, where the Nepal Army has begun installation; Trishuli Bazaar and Betrawati, each needing about a 48 m span; and Syabrubesi, needing about 75 m. Moving the components is hampered because the lower road sections are still blocked. China has supplied Bailey components at the Korala border for possible use at Rasuwagadhi.

Named bridges destroyed: Betrawati old and new; the Trishuli River bridge at Tupche; Trishuli Bazar old and new; Simchaur; the bridge near the Water Resources and Irrigation Division at Devighat; a Mid-Hill Highway bridge; two on the Tadi Khola; Shreekali, Budhsinghghat, Ratamate and Phosretar over the Trishuli; and in Dhading the Syaltar road bridge, Ghatbesi bridge, Phurke Khola bridge at Malekhu and two on the Kolpu Khola.

Bridge totals are not reconciled across sources. NDRRMA reported 41 motorable bridges washed away and 4 more damaged; OnlineKhabar counted at least 19 bridges and about 40 km of road along the Trishuli corridor; the Department of Roads early estimate was 68 suspension and 33 driveable bridges damaged, with an initial Rs 15 bn estimate for road and bridge infrastructure.

Electricity, district level: Rasuwa 78% of 14,281 affected households restored, Nuwakot 96.7% of 68,679, Dhading 99.8% of 83,642 with about 120 families still dark. Rasuwa floods affected roughly 10% of Nepal's total generation capacity.

Water supply: 55 drinking-water projects damaged across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Gorkha, with Rs 640 m estimated damage; Nuwakot is worst hit with 22 projects affected. The Bidur Water Supply Project runs on a 100 kVA diesel generator distributing about 500,000 litres a day.

UNICEF reported at least 22,000 children in the flood-affected areas without safe drinking water, sanitation and hygiene support, and dispatched supplies for about 19,000 people in Rasuwa and Nuwakot.

Telecommunications: Nepal Telecom restored 116 of 120 affected towers by 1 September using helicopter-carried crews. Ncell restored 24 of 27, leaving Ghattekhola and Timure in Rasuwa and Trishuli/Bidur in Nuwakot down; 60 km of fibre was damaged and total telecom infrastructure damage is put at Rs 450 m.

Displacement: 3,458 people were living in 27 displacement sites in Nuwakot and Rasuwa, mostly in schools, as of 1 September. IOM's Displacement Tracking Matrix covers 15 sites in Dhading, Nuwakot and Rasuwa and estimates 4,288 households affected, of which 2,886 displaced.

Cross-border: the Gyirong checkpoint on the Chinese side was destroyed, along with a 5 km stretch of China National Highway 216 toward Rasuwagadhi, and communications and power to the Gyirong Port area were cut. About 80 trucks and 170 containers were stranded in Gyirong town. On the Nepal side the Rasuwagadhi customs office was destroyed and more than 300 vehicles plus roughly 1,000 electric vehicles awaiting export were swept away.

Health facilities: Syafrubesi and Timure health posts, the Timure health desk and the Mailung community health unit were fully damaged; Baireni Hospital in Galchhi and the Charadhuli basic health service centre were partially damaged; access to Dhading and Trishuli hospitals was disrupted. Nineteen schools were surveyed across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, covering 6,901 enrolled students: eight fully damaged, eight partially damaged, three safe.

Shelter: 30 holding centres held 3,930 people, 19 centres and 2,653 people in Nuwakot and 11 centres and 1,277 people in Rasuwa. In Nuwakot 1,267 houses were fully damaged and 1,253 partially damaged. Satellite mapping put 4,689 buildings inside the flood zone, an exposure estimate rather than verified damage.

Nuwakot agriculture, preliminary: 4,440 ropani of crops affected, 2,035 livestock and 16,500 birds lost. Two wastewater treatment plants were destroyed at Dhunge and Bidur, and 465 further households were affected across the Trishuli Colony, Devighat and Betrawati water schemes.

Krishnabhir remains fully closed on the Prithvi Highway (about 300 m of road collapsed on 30 August). Department of Roads Director General Bijaya Jaisi said a decision on whether vehicles can pass through will come within a week. Two long-term bypass options are under study: twin 500 m tunnels, or two permanent bridges rerouting the highway across the Trishuli River and back, with repairing the existing road the first priority. Two detours are in use: a Galchhi route via a bridge near "Hamlet Restaurant" along the opposite riverbank (about 20 km, to Parewatar), and a Chitwan-side route via the Fishling and Benighat bridges (about 17.5 km, with a 1.5 km stretch still under repair).
